title: We are not Hindus
hook: Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's book argued Sikhi was distinct, while honoring neighbors

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khalsa College, and your line was a college for the khalsa. What did you learn and pass on? This week ran from pardesi through the Sabhas, Ditt Singh, Gurmukh Singh and a college. It ends with a book. Day nine hundred sixty-six.

A book title can sound like a slammed door. This one, in Punjabi, is Ham Hindu Nahin: we are not Hindus. Read only the cover and you might expect an attack. Open it, and the author starts somewhere else. He's writing to his Hindu neighbors and friends with respect, he says, and he means them no ill will. He simply wants to set down, plainly, from the Gurus' own words, what makes the Sikh path its own. The author is Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha. Today: we are not Hindus.
screen: `A TITLE LIKE A SLAMMED DOOR.` → `OPEN IT: RESPECT FIRST.` → `BHAI KAHN SINGH OF NABHA.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In the years of the Singh Sabhas, a debate ran through the Punjab: were Sikhs a separate faith, or a branch of the wider Hindu family? Some Hindu reformers held that Sikhs belonged within the Hindu fold, and some Sikhs agreed. Other Sikhs disagreed sharply. Feelings ran high on every side. Second, the scholar. Kahn Singh was a learned man from the princely state of Nabha, at home in Punjabi, Persian and the old texts. He answered the question the way a scholar does: not with insults, but with quotations. Page after page, he set the Gurus' hymns beside the claim, and let the hymns speak. Third, his evidence. The Sikhs, he argued, have their own Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib; their own initiation, the Khalsa's amrit; their own rites for birth, marriage and death; their own places of worship. And he pointed to the Gurus themselves, including the hymn you met at the family table some days ago: Guru Arjan, in Bhairo, saying he is neither Hindu nor Muslim, and that his body and breath belong to the One whom some call Allah and some call Ram. Kahn Singh read it as the Gurus marking out a path of their own. Fourth, the kindness. In the Punjab, some Sikh and Hindu families were kin, sharing weddings, festivals and grief. Kahn Singh's book draws a line around the Sikh path, but it doesn't push the neighbors away. That balance is today's line. Hindus, of course, describe their own traditions in their own words, and this lesson isn't the place to describe them. It's about how one Sikh scholar said who his community was. His book is one picture of saying clearly who you are while still sitting at a neighbor's table.
screen: `SEPARATE FAITH, OR A BRANCH?` · `A SCHOLAR'S ANSWER: QUOTATIONS.` · `OWN GURU, RITES AND PLACES.` · `A LINE THAT DOESN'T PUSH AWAY.` · then, large: `DISTINCT, AND KIND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for saying who you are. Sit, and let your breath slow. Finish this sentence quietly, in your own words: I am someone who… Let one honest answer come: a faith, a practice, a value, a place you belong. Now picture saying it to a neighbor who sees the world differently. Say it again in your head, with the same words, but warmer. Notice that the truth didn't change, only the tone. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between the breaths. The bell holds the time.
Kahn Singh, the scholar of Nabha who wrote Ham Hindu Nahin, setting out from the Gurus' words what makes Sikhi distinct, while honoring Hindu neighbors. Today's word.
Your line: distinct, and kind. Today, state who you are, plainly and kindly, to someone who might see it differently. Day nine hundred sixty-six.
